ddx.step1_summary:
• Chief complaint: 3-day history of ‘bad diarrhoea’.
• Symptoms: 4–5 bowel motions/day, loose to watery; mild lower abdominal pain; single vomiting episode; possible low-grade fever; ↓ appetite. No blood or mucus. No recent travel or suspicious food; able to maintain oral fluids. No meds taken for diarrhoea or pain so far.
• Past medical history: asthma (uses an inhaler – patient calls it “Lexapro,” unclear). No other chronic illness noted.
• Medications / allergies: Inhaler named “Lexapro” (likely mis-named); no known drug allergies.
• Family / social history: Father hypertensive, died of bowel cancer at 62. No social habits provided (smoke/alcohol not discussed).
• Vital signs / exam: Not recorded; clinician notes patient “doesn’t look dehydrated.” No physical exam findings supplied.
• Labs / imaging: None obtained or mentioned.

V: Ischemic colitis: sudden diarrhoea can occur with vascular compromise, but lack of blood and mild presentation make it less likely.
Mesenteric ischemia (acute): also causes pain/diarrhoea, but severity expected to be higher.
I: Viral gastroenteritis (e.g., norovirus/rotavirus): classic short, self-limited watery diarrhoea with vomiting and low-grade fever.
Bacterial gastroenteritis / food-borne illness (e.g., Salmonella, Campylobacter, ETEC): similar acute presentation; may or may not have blood; often 3–5 days.
Clostridioides difficile colitis: possible if prior antibiotics, but none reported.
N: Colorectal cancer: family history; can produce change in bowel habit, but usually chronic and may include blood/weight loss.
D: Lactase deficiency (lactose intolerance): can cause diarrhoea after dairy; patient denies dairy trigger currently.
Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency: chronic greasy stools rather than acute watery.
I2: Medication-induced diarrhoea (SSRI / ‘Lexapro’ – escitalopram): recognised adverse effect.
Food-borne toxin (pre-formed toxin such as S. aureus): brief vomiting/diarrhoea episode.
A: Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn’s/UC): diarrhoea +/- blood, but generally chronic; can present acutely during flare.
E: Hyperthyroidism: can cause diarrhoea, but other symptoms absent.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Most common cause of short-duration watery diarrhoea with mild systemic features in otherwise healthy adults; fits timeline and self-limiting nature.
supporting_evidence: No travel or antibiotic use needed—community viruses common
opposing_evidence: None strong; lack of clear sick contacts or outbreak information (but not required)

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Several bacteria cause similar self-limited illness; slightly less likely because patient denies suspicious food or travel but still possible from routine meals.
supporting_evidence: Acute onset watery diarrhoea with mild abdominal pain
Illness duration in typical 3–7 day window
opposing_evidence: No high-risk foods, travel, or outbreak history

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Escitalopram commonly causes gastrointestinal upset; unclear if patient actually uses SSRI, but possible mis-naming of inhaler.
supporting_evidence: Medications are a frequent cause of new-onset diarrhoea
opposing_evidence: Likely chronic use rather than new start (would expect earlier symptoms)
Symptom cluster (vomit, fever) favours infectious aetiology

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Functional disorder can flare intermittently, but usually chronic; infection-type symptoms (vomit, fever) less characteristic.
supporting_evidence: History of intermittent loose stools after certain foods/travel

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Could present with diarrhoea and abdominal pain, but absence of blood/mucus and no prior diagnosis makes it less probable.
supporting_evidence: Family GI malignancy (not directly IBD but raises colon pathology vigilance)
opposing_evidence: No blood, mucus, weight loss or chronic symptoms
